(p-487) Surah al-Mujadila

It is Medinan by the consensus of all, except for a report from ʿAtaʾ that its first ten verses are Medinan and the rest are Meccan.

Al-Kalbi said: all of it was revealed in Medina except for His words, exalted is He: ﴿There is no secret conversation among three but that He is their fourth﴾, which was revealed in Mecca.

Her husband was Aws ibn al-Samit.

ʿUrwa said: he was a man afflicted with madness (lamam), and some of his madness struck him, so he made a ẓihār against his wife, and she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking him for a ruling on that matter.

﴿And she complains to Allah﴾: concerning this there are two interpretations:

The first: she seeks help from Allah.

The second: she asks Allah for mercy.

Al-Hasan narrated that she said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah has abrogated the customs of the Jahiliyya, and my husband has made ẓihār against me." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Nothing has been revealed to me about this." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, has revelation come to you concerning everything and this has been hidden from you?" He said: "It is as I have told you." She said: "I complain to Allah, not to His Messenger." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who pleads with you﴾, the verse.

Ibn Masʿud recited: ﴿Qad samiʿa﴾ (with the verb in the form). ʿAʾisha said: "Blessed is Allah whose hearing encompasses everything. He heard the speech of Khawla bint Thaʿlaba, and I was in a corner of the house, not hearing some of what she says, and she was saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, my youth has been consumed, my children have ended, and I have exhausted my womb for him; but when my age grew old, he made ẓihār against me. O Allah, I complain to You.' She had not yet left until Jibril came down with this verse."

﴿And Allah hears your mutual discourse; indeed Allah is Hearing, Seeing﴾. The muhawara (mutual discourse) is the return of speech. ʿAntara said:

"Had she known what mutual discourse is, she would have complained, and had he known speech, my interlocutor would have spoken."

﴿Those of you who make ẓihār of their wives﴾: ẓihār (the pre-Islamic repudiation formula) is a man's saying to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother." It was called ẓihār because he intended to make her back forbidden to him, and it was said: because he made her to him like the back of his mother. In the Jahiliyya it was a threefold divorce with no possibility of return and no permission after it, so Allah abrogated it to what the Sharia settled upon, namely the obligation of expiation (kaffara) for it upon return (al-ʿawd).

Then He said, ﴿They are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who bore them﴾, as a refutation by God Most High of the man's saying to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother" (anta ʿalayya ka-ẓahri ummi).

﴿And indeed they utter an objectionable word and a falsehood﴾. He means by "objectionable word" the apparent (al-ẓāhir) one, and by "falsehood" their lie in making wives into mothers.

Then He said, ﴿They are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who bore them﴾, as a refutation by God Most High of the man's saying to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother" (anta ʿalayya ka-ẓahri ummi).

﴿And indeed they utter an objectionable word and a falsehood﴾. He means by "objectionable word" the apparent (al-ẓāhir) one, and by "falsehood" their lie in making wives into mothers.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 58, verses 5–7:

﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ has two interpretations:

First: they show enmity to Allah and His Messenger; this is the view of Mujahid.

Second: they oppose Allah and His Messenger; this is the view of al-Kalbi.

Regarding the root meaning of al-muhadda (opposition), there are two views:

First: that it is being on one boundary (hadd) that differs from the boundary of your companion; this is said by al-Zajjaj.

Second: that it is derived from iron prepared for opposition (al-muhadda), i.e., iron made ready for combat.

﴿Be humiliated, as those before them were humiliated﴾ has four interpretations:

First: [they were disgraced] as those before them were disgraced; this is said by Qatadah.

Second: its meaning is "they were destroyed as those before them were destroyed"; this is said by al-Akhfash and Abu Ubayda.

Third: "they were cursed as those before them were cursed"; this is said by al-Suddi, and it was said that it is in the dialect of Madhhij.

(p-490) Fourth: "they were turned back, subdued."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 58, verses 8–10:

﴿Have you not considered those who were forbidden from secret counsel (al-najwa)?﴾ Al-najwa is secret discourse (al-sirar). From this is the verse of Jarir:

"From the fair-faced company who, when they hold secret counsel, the Lu'ayy ibn Ghalib are made to confess their secret."

Al-najwa is derived from al-najwa (elevation), meaning that which is elevated and distant, because those present are far from it. Regarding it there are two views:

First: every secret conversation is najwa. This was said by Ibn Isa.

Second: sirar is what occurs between two persons, and najwa is what occurs among three. This was related by Suraqa.

Regarding those who were forbidden, there are three opinions:

First: they were the Jews, who would hold secret counsel about the Muslims, so they were forbidden from that. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: they were the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). This was said by al-Kalbi.

Third: they were the Muslims.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that he said: "One night we were conversing when the Messenger of Allah (p-491) (ﷺ) came out to us and said: (What is this secret counsel? Were you not forbidden from secret counsel?) We said: 'We repent to Allah, O Messenger of Allah. We were speaking about the Messiah, meaning the Dajjal, out of fear of him.' He said: (Shall I not inform you of something that I fear for you more than him?) They said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: (Hidden shirk: that a man stands up to perform an action so that another man may see him.)"

﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with that by which Allah has not greeted you.﴾ "When the Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) they would say: 'As-sam almu 'alayka' (death be upon you), and the Prophet (ﷺ) would return the greeting, saying: 'And upon you.'" It is also related that when Aisha heard this from them she said: "And upon you be as-sam and adh-dham," and he, peace be upon him, said: (Indeed Allah does not love obscenity or the use of obscene speech.)

Regarding the as-sam which they intended, there are three opinions:

First: it is death. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Second: it is the sword.

Third: they meant by it that you will become weary of your religion. This was said by al-Hasan, and likewise whoever said it is death, because one who dies becomes weary of life.

Al-Kalbi related that the Jews, when the Prophet (ﷺ) returned the greeting of their salutation, would say: "If this were a prophet, his words 'and upon you' would be answered for him among us," meaning as-sam, which is death; "and we are not weary, nor is there lassitude in our bodies." So there was revealed concerning them: ﴿And they say to themselves: Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?﴾ and the verse.

Concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Secret counsel is only from Satan, so that he may grieve those who believe﴾ there are two views:

First: what the Jews and hypocrites would confer about, of rumours against the Muslims.

Second: that it refers to the dreams which a person sees in his sleep and which cause him grief.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 58, verse 11:

﴿O you who have believed, when you are told, "Make space in the assemblies,"﴾ there are four interpretations regarding it:

The first: the assembly of the Prophet ﷺ specifically, when a people sit in it and compete for their places, so that when someone enters upon them, they should give him preference over themselves or make room for him. So they were commanded to do this. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: that it refers to the assemblies of the Friday prayer. This is the view of Muqatil.

The third: that it refers to all assemblies of remembrance (dhikr). This is the view of Qatadah.

The fourth: that this concerns warfare and fighting. This is the view of al-Hasan.

﴿And when you are told, "Rise up, then rise up,"﴾ there are four interpretations regarding it:

The first: its meaning is, "And when you are told to stand up for fighting, then stand up." This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: "When you are called to good, then respond." This is the view of Qatadah.

The third: "When the call is made to prayer, then hasten to it." This is the view of Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

The fourth: that when they sat in the house of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they would prolong their sitting so that each one of them would be the last to leave his presence. So Allah commanded them that when they were told, "Rise up," they should rise. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The meaning of ﴿tafassahu﴾ is "make room" (tawassa'u).

Regarding ﴿unshuzu﴾ there are two meanings:

The first: its meaning is "stand up" (qumu). This is the view of Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: "rise up," derived from *nashz al-ard* (elevated ground), which is its height.

Regarding that to which they were commanded to rise, there are three interpretations:

The first: to the prayer. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

The second: to the military campaign. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: to every good. This is the view of Qatadah.

﴿Allah will raise those who have believed among you﴾ meaning: by their faith, above those who are not of their standing in faith.

﴿and those who have been given knowledge, by degrees﴾ above those who are not scholars.

(p-493) This may bear two meanings:

The first: that it is an informative statement about their state with Allah in the Hereafter.

The second: that it is a command that elevates them in the assemblies mentioned earlier, arranging people in them according to their merits in religion and knowledge.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah 58, verses 12–13:**

﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger privately, spend something in charity before your private consultation.﴾ There are three opinions regarding its occasion (sabab al-nuzul):

The first: The hypocrites used to consult the Prophet ﷺ privately about things for which they had no need. So Allah commanded them to give charity before private consultation, so as to cut them off from private consultation. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: A group of Muslims used to take the Prophet ﷺ aside and consult him privately. Some other Muslims suspected them of belittling them in these private consultations, and this distressed them. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded them to give charity before private consultation, so as to cut them off from monopolizing his time. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The Muslims asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so many questions that they wearied him. Allah wished to lighten the burden on His Prophet, so when this command was revealed, many of the people refrained from asking.

Mujahid said: No one consulted him privately except 'Ali, who offered a dinar and gave it in charity, and then asked him about ten matters. Then the concession was revealed.

﴿Are you apprehensive about spending charity before your private consultation?﴾ 'Ali said: No one acted upon it except me, until it was abrogated (nusikhat). I think he [i.e., 'Ali] said: It lasted only an hour. Ibn Hibban said: This continued for ten nights.

Ibn Sulayman said: 'Ali consulted him privately with a dinar, which he had sold for ten dirhams, and asked ten questions, each question for one dirham.

Another of the Ansar consulted him with several ṣā' (a measure of grain), and spoke several words, and then it was abrogated by what came after it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 58, verses 14–19:

﴿Have you not considered those who have taken as allies a people with whom Allah is angry?﴾ This means the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) who took as allies a people with whom Allah is angry; they are the Jews.

﴿They are neither of you nor of them﴾ because of their hypocrisy (nifaq).

﴿Nor of them﴾ because of their departure with their Judaism.

﴿And they swear by a lie﴾ that they have not been hypocrites.

﴿While they know﴾ that they are hypocrites.

﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield, and so they averted [others] from the way of Allah; for them is a humiliating punishment.﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: this was said by al-Suddi.

The second: "from the way of Allah" refers to their being killed for disbelief when they displayed the hypocrisy they had concealed.

It may also bear a third meaning: they averted [others] from jihad, inclining toward the Jews.

﴿Shaytan has overcome them﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: he became strong over them.

The second: he encompassed them; this was said by al-Mufaddal.

And there is a third: that he prevailed and gained control over them in this world.

(p-495) ﴿So he made them forget the remembrance of Allah﴾ The "remembrance of Allah" here may have two meanings:

The first: His commands to obey Him in action.

The second: His prohibitions warning against disobeying Him.

And the phrase "what made them forget His remembrance" may bear two meanings:

The first: by heedlessness of it.

The second: by associating others with it (shirk).

﴿Have you not considered those who have taken as allies a people with whom Allah is angry?﴾ This means the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) who took as allies a people with whom Allah is angry; they are the Jews.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 58, verses 20–22:

﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾. In this there are three meanings:

First: those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Farra'.

Second: those who defy Allah and His Messenger. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

Third: those who show enmity to Allah and His Messenger. This is the view of Muqatil.

﴿Even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their clan﴾. Scholars differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, giving three opinions:

The first: what Ibn Shawdhab said, that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, who killed his father, al-Jarrah, on the day of Badr. His father kept confronting him while Abu Ubaydah kept turning away from him, until, when he persisted, Abu Ubaydah went straight for him and killed him.

(p-496) Sa'id ibn Abd al-Aziz narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "If Abu Ubaydah were alive, he would have appointed him (as a leader)." Sa'id said: "And concerning him this verse was revealed."

In this verse there are two possibilities:

One: it is in the form of a prohibition addressed to the believers, that they should not love those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.

Two: it is in the form of a description of them and a praise, that they do not love those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, and this is praise.

﴿Those are the ones in whose hearts He has written faith﴾. In this there are four meanings:

First: its meaning is that He placed faith in their hearts and established it. Al-Suddi said: "So it became like something written down."

Second: He wrote in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the heavenly record) that faith is in their hearts.

Third: He judged that their hearts possess faith.

Fourth: He placed in their hearts a mark (sign) of faith, indicating that they are among the people of faith. This was related by Ibn Isa.

﴿And He strengthened them with a spirit from Himself﴾. In this there are five meanings:

First: He aided them with His mercy. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Second: He strengthened them with His help until they gained victory.

Third: He made them desire the Qur'an until they believed.

Fourth: He strengthened them with the light of guidance until they were patient.

Fifth: He strengthened them with Jibril on the day of Badr.

﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾, meaning in this world, through their obedience.

﴿And they are pleased with Him﴾. In this there are two meanings:

One: they are pleased with Him in the Hereafter, through the reward.

Two: they are pleased with Him in this world with what He decreed for them, so they did not dislike it.

﴿Those are the party of Allah﴾. Concerning them there are two meanings: (p-497)
One: they are of the followers of Allah, so no blame of any blamer will affect them.

Two: they are the helpers of His truth and the guardians of His creation. This is a possible meaning.

The second opinion: what Ibn Jurayj related, that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. He had "heard his father, Abu Quhafah, insult the Prophet (ﷺ), so Abu Bakr struck him a blow that made him fall on his face. He mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) said: 'Did you really do that? Do not do it again, Abu Bakr.' Abu Bakr said: 'By Allah, if the sword were near me, I would have struck him with it.' Then this verse was revealed."

The third opinion: what al-Kalbi and Muqatil related, that this verse was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, who had written to the people of Makkah warning them of the march of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against them in the year of the Conquest.
